confirmed.title: Sign-in throttles on the second-factor step are kept in each task's memory, so the per-IP TOTP guessing budget doubles, and nothing counts wrong authenticator codes per account
confirmed.mechanism: Every throttle on /api/auth/mfa/verify and /api/auth/enterprise/verify-mfa is an in-process counter: express-rate-limit's default MemoryStore (mfaLimiter, enterpriseAuthLimiter, rateLimiters.auth), and redisRateLimiter's `memoryStore` Map, which is always used because REDIS_URL is unset. The ALB has no stickiness and round-robins across the 2 API tasks, so each task keeps its own count and the effective per-IP ceiling is 2x the configured one (for example mfaLimiter goes from 10 to 20 per 15 minutes). For an account with an authenticator enrolled, a wrong TOTP at the login challenge is not counted against the account. verifySecondFactor/consumeTotpStep only stop replay. Compare the password step, which calls recordFailedLogin (a DB lockout at 5), and the e-signature pre-checks, which call allowance.recordFailedAttempt. The per-IP in-memory limiter is therefore the only brake on second-factor guessing at sign-in, and multi-task deployment splits it.
confirmed.client_failure: No visible failure for a legitimate user. The risk is weaker account security: someone who already holds a user's password gets twice as many authenticator-code guesses per IP per window as configured (and as many again per extra task at scale-out), with no per-account lockout ever triggering. The emailed-OTP path is not affected because verifyEmailOtp caps attempts at 5 in the users row.
confirmed.reachability: Reached by sign-in (launch catalog, account security): POST /api/auth/login followed by /api/auth/mfa/verify, and the enterprise 3-step flow, for any account with mfa_enabled + mfa_method='totp'. Certain for the doubling (2 API tasks, no stickiness, no Redis). The missing per-account TOTP counter is present in a single process too; only the doubling is specific to multi-task.
confirmed.mitigations_checked: Password guesses: DB lockout (auth-security-service isAccountLocked/recordFailedLogin), shared across tasks. Mitigated. Email OTP: 5-attempt cap in users.email_otp_attempts via atomic UPDATE. Mitigated. TOTP replay: users.mfa_totp_last_step conditional UPDATE. Mitigated. E-signature password/MFA pre-checks and the signing ceremony record failures into the same DB lockout. Mitigated, even though signing-attempt-limiter.ts is itself per task. No Redis store for express-rate-limit and no production refusal when Redis is absent.

confirmed.title: Authoring presence roster lives in one task's memory: co-authors vanish on about half of heartbeats and everywhere after each deploy

confirmed.title: Nightly memory consolidation runs at 02:00:00 on all three tasks at once and writes each conversation memory into AnA's project memory three times
confirmed.mechanism: registerProjectRoutes calls initMemoryConsolidationScheduler() on every boot with no env or role gate, so all three processes (2 API tasks and the worker) set up the same node-cron job. The cron fires on the wall clock, so all three start runConsolidation() within milliseconds of each other at 02:00 UTC. Each process runs findStaleMemories at about the same moment, and because the only guard against re-consolidation is a NOT EXISTS read, all three get the same batch of 50 cwm rows. For each row, every process then reads the 50 most recent existing memories for the acceptance gate's dedupe and contradiction check, waits on an OpenAI embedding call (hundreds of ms), and only then INSERTs. The processes stay in lockstep, so each one's gate read finishes before any other process's insert lands, and the gate's content dedupe does not trigger. project_memory_entries has no unique constraint on (project_id, title) or on content; the only indexes are on org, project and (project, category), per migrations/20260331_performance_indexes.sql:248-264. There is no advisory lock, no leader election and no role check.
confirmed.client_failure: Every summary AnA distils from a project conversation is stored three times as identical 'conversation_summary' rows with identical embeddings. Semantic recall (client-intelligence-memory.ts:1327-1341, ORDER BY embedding <=> query LIMIT n) then returns the same memory three times in a row, which pushes other distinct project memories out of AnA's context. The client sees AnA recall less of the project history and repeat the same remembered fact. The embedding spend for this job is also tripled every night. A single local process never shows this, because the NOT EXISTS guard is correct for one runner.
confirmed.reachability: Certain that the job starts in production: it is mounted unconditionally from registerPostStartRoutes -> registerProjectRoutes, and OPENAI_API_KEY is set, so embedding succeeds and makes the race window wider. confirmed.mitigations_checked: No pg_advisory_lock or leader election anywhere in this module; advisory locks in the server exist only in credit-ledger.ts, audit/chain.ts and tamper-proof-audit.ts. No unique index on project_memory_entries. The memory-acceptance gate's dedupe reads existing rows before the concurrent inserts commit, so it cannot see them. No REDIS_URL-based lock. votes.reason: I could not refute this. The job is registered unconditionally on every process. Nothing serializes it: no advisory lock, no leader election, no role or env gate, no unique constraint. Its only guards against running twice are reads taken before the other processes commit their inserts: the NOT EXISTS in findStaleMemories and the acceptance gate's dedupe_key comparison. All three tasks run the same image and command, so each schedules '0 2 * * *' on its own clock, and those clocks are NTP-synced. Each task selects the same oldest 50 rows in the same ORDER BY and then inserts after an OpenAI embedding call that takes hundreds of milliseconds. A task only sees another's row, and its dedupe only rejects it, if that task started later by more than the embedding latency. Tasks that start within milliseconds of each other will each insert the same 'Conversation summary ... [cwm_N]' row, so you get up to three copies. How many duplicates appear on a given night depends on timing drift across the batch. That makes 'three times, every row' an upper bound rather than a certainty, but duplication does happen. Recall does not remove the copies: the RAG path runs with useMmr:false and useReranking:false, and the direct fallback is a plain ORDER BY embedding <=> LIMIT, so identical rows crowd out distinct memories. Severity stays medium: this is persistent pollution of AnA project memory plus tripled embedding cost. No governed content or audit trail is lost.

If the processes drift apart over the per-row embedding latency, a slower process's gate read (the 50 most recent entries, content dedupe) may see a faster process's committed insert and reject the duplicate. confirmed.title: Schedule-of-events sweep runs on every task: health-review revisions are always tripled, and recovery tasks and slip alerts duplicate when sweeps overlap
confirmed.mechanism: startScheduleOfEventsSweep() runs in all three processes (disabled only by NODE_ENV=test or SCHEDULE_OF_EVENTS_SWEEP_DISABLED, neither of which is set in production), every 6 h from each process's own boot. (1) Deterministic: every process's pass calls recordRevision('health_review') unconditionally for every active schedule, so each project's schedule revision history gets 3 'Proactive review' rows per 6 h instead of 1. (2) Racy: the notify-once guard is a read-check-write on the metadata JSON (lastNotifiedStatus), and the task dedupe is SELECT-then-INSERT (hasOpenScheduleTask) with no unique constraint. When two processes' passes over the same project overlap, both read the old metadata, both open a 'Recover slipped milestone' task, and both insert a 'Milestone slipped' mdx_notifications row. Unlike taskDueSweep, which claims the row with a guarded UPDATE ... RETURNING before notifying, this has no claim step.

The two API tasks, launched together by ECS, can boot within seconds of each other, and a trailing process that skips already-handled writes can catch up to the leader. Still, this is timing-dependent and I have not observed it. Rate the duplicate-task part as plausible rather than confirmed.
confirmed.mitigations_checked: No advisory lock, leader election or role gate in scheduleOfEventsSweep.ts or service.ts. No unique index on project_tasks (metadata source/milestoneKey/kind) or on mdx_notifications (only non-unique indexes in migrations/20260510_notifications_and_clinical.sql:40-44). rejected.title: Every deploy cuts in-flight AnA turns after about 40 s. The run row stays 'running' for up to 5 minutes and the client blames the network

The finding's central consequence, that the ana_runs row stays 'running' for up to 5 minutes until the reaper finds it, does not happen as configured. The stream route registers a disconnect handler on both res and req 'close'. The handler calls stopRunInternally, which aborts the local run straight away and writes status='cancelled', stopped_reason='client_disconnected'. In an ECS rolling replacement the ALB drains the old target for deregistration_delay (30 s). Any SSE connection still open when that delay ends is closed by the ALB. ECS sends SIGTERM only after deregistration has finished, so the socket 'close' fires, and the row is settled, while the process and its DB pool are still alive. Graceful shutdown then waits up to another 10 s before pool.end(). The reaper is only a backstop for a hard kill, not the path a deploy takes.

Because the row is terminal, the follow-on claims also fall away. A later Stop gets 'Run already cancelled' (409), not a silently accepted write. A pending approval is refused for the same reason: the approval path checks cancelSignal and records client_disconnected with 'The connection dropped before anyone decided, so this action did not run.'

The client-side claim is overstated too. The 'AnA is unreachable' text appears only when no text had streamed yet (m.text.length > 0 ? m.text : ...). A partial answer stays on screen, marked interrupted.

What remains is generic: a rolling deploy ends an SSE response that runs longer than the drain window, and the partial assistant text is not saved to the thread. The code already handles that case honestly, as an interrupted turn with an audited client_disconnected, and it is not the 5-minute stale-run defect the finding describes.

rejected.title: eCTD package download (POST /api/ectd/export/:id) re-assembles synchronously and records a governed export and a Part 11 'ectd_export_generated' audit event before sending the bytes. On a CloudFront 504 the trail shows an export that nobody received

votes.reason:
The finding has two parts: a CloudFront 504 on a slow export, and audit and governance records written for a package nobody received. Neither is confirmed as a separate production defect.

1. The timeout is plausible but not shown. The ALB origin in terraform/modules/cloudfront/main.tf (custom_origin_config, around lines 132-147) sets no origin_read_timeout, so CloudFront's 30 s default applies. But nothing shows that an export takes longer than 30 s. The finding admits the duration was never measured. The export button only renders after a compile that returned in time. Compile does almost the same work: compileFromSpine in server/routes/ectd-compile.ts (around line 976) calls assembleSequence, the same assembler the export reaches through assembleSubmissionEctd (server/services/ectd/assemble-from-core.ts:568). The only extra export work is validateEctdPackage and one hash. So the failing case needs compile to finish just under 30 s and export to finish just over it, or leaf content to grow between the two calls. That is speculation. Any real timeout exposure belongs to the compile/assembly-duration finding, not to this one.

2. The "false audit trail" claim does not hold. The audit action is 'ectd_export_generated', and the package really was generated. The handler deliberately writes it before sending, with a comment saying so (ectd-export.ts:604-606: "Audit the export BEFORE returning the buffer. Even if the response stream fails downstream, the user-requested generation is the §11.10(e) event we need to record."). registerExportGovernanceQuick documents the same order ("Call this AFTER the export buffer is ready but BEFORE sending the response", exportGovernance.ts:333). The sha256 on both records is the digest of the bytes that were really produced (ectd-export.ts:580). Nothing records a delivery that did not happen: the records describe a server-side generation that did happen. Retries producing several records with different hashes are several real generations, each recorded truthfully. The compile path already writes audit rows the same way (assembleSequence recordAuditRow at assemble-from-core.ts:203 and :365). The Part 11 record of a user-initiated action is not wrong or missing, so there is no audit-trail gap.

3. The mismatch is not specific to production. Recording before send means any client disconnect, network drop or tab close leaves the same "generated but not received" state in a local run. Production does not create that mismatch; it only adds a possible timeout trigger, and that trigger is not shown to fire.

What remains is a possible 504 and a retry on a slow export, already covered by the compile/assembly-duration finding. It is not a separate audit-integrity defect.

votes.reason:
It is true that no pipeline rolls the worker. The claimed failure, though, needs an image in the `worker` ECR repo, and nothing in the repository ever puts one there. The worker task definition pulls `${module.ecr.repository_urls["worker"]}:${var.image_tag}`, which is a separate, IMMUTABLE-tag repo. deploy-aws.yml pushes only `c2c-prod-api`. The old worker build step targeted `worker/Dockerfile`, which never existed, so it failed every time and never pushed anything. No script, workflow or Terraform code pushes to or retags into the worker repo. As configured, `terraform apply` produces a worker service whose image tag does not exist, so the task fails to pull and never runs. The finding concedes this: "If the worker repo lacks the tag, the service simply never starts."

The skew scenario therefore requires an out-of-band manual push that the repo neither performs nor documents. The concrete client harm cited needs a worker image from before 2026-09-21, and that is unreachable. No worker image was ever built by any pipeline. Production has also never been applied: LAUNCH_DEFINITION_OF_DONE D1 says "nothing applied" as of 2026-09-24. So any worker image a person could push now would contain the post-fix audit writer.

The real defect underneath is a different one: a worker service that is either dead or a duplicate copy of the full server with all its schedulers. That belongs to the duplicate-scheduler or readiness findings. Version skew over time is not what happens under the code as written.
